common_name: Autumnalis Rosea Higan Cherry (Deep Pink Fall-Blooming Ornamental Cherry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Autumnalis Rosea is a pink-flowered sport of Autumnalis and shares its habit of producing a partial flush of flowers in mild fall and winter weather in addition to its main spring bloom.

directions: Autumnalis Rosea is a deeper-pink-flowered form of the fall-blooming Higan cherry, carrying semi-double flowers of a noticeably richer rose-pink than the pale-pink species cultivar Autumnalis, appearing intermittently through fall and mild winter stretches whenever temperatures rise enough to trigger a flush, then finishing with a fuller display in early spring. The rounded, twiggy, upright-spreading canopy is identical to Autumnalis in form and vigor, and the tree shares the same cold hardiness and longevity advantages over the showier double-flowered spring-only cherries. Grow it in full sun on moist, well-drained soil, and expect the fall flowering to be sparser and more sporadic than the concentrated spring flush, varying from year to year with autumn weather patterns.

common_name: Emerald Lustre Viburnum (Extra-Glossy Large-Leaved Sweet Viburnum)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Emerald Lustre is selected for especially large, deeply glossed foliage and shares the species' rapid growth rate, reaching a dense screen or small tree of 15-20 feet if left unpruned.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Emerald Lustre is a selection of sweet viburnum chosen for its exceptionally large, thick, deeply glossed dark-green leaves, which give the foliage a more refined, lacquered appearance than the straight species. It shares sweet viburnum's fragrant white flower panicles in spring, red-to-black fruit clusters, and rapid growth into a dense evergreen screen or hedge 10-20 feet tall. Shearing 2-3 times per year maintains it as a tight formal hedge, while left unpruned it develops into a handsome large multi-stemmed shrub with the same glossy, high-shine leaf display that gives the cultivar its name. Reliable from zone 8b southward and damaged by temperatures below 15F, same as the species.

common_name: Little Plum Lewisia (Compact Magenta-Flowered Alpine Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring at a slight angle into an extremely well-drained, gritty crevice or trough in full sun; Little Plum is a compact garden hybrid bred from L. longipetala and tolerates a bit more summer moisture than most evergreen lewisias while still needing sharp drainage.

directions: Little Plum is a compact, free-flowering hybrid derived from Lewisia longipetala, bred by alpine specialists in the Pacific Northwest for garden vigor and an extended bloom season. It forms small, glossy evergreen rosettes topped from late spring into summer, and often intermittently beyond, with rich plum-magenta to deep rose-pink flowers held just above the foliage on short stems. Because of its longipetala parentage it tolerates somewhat more consistent moisture during the growing season than most evergreen lewisia hybrids, though it still demands sharp drainage and resents standing water at the crown. Grow it in a crevice, trough, or raised scree bed with full sun, watering a bit more generously in spring than other Lewisia species while avoiding soggy conditions.

common_name: Little Mango Lewisia (Compact Apricot-Orange-Flowered Alpine Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown starts in spring at a slight angle into an extremely well-drained, gritty crevice or trough in full sun; Little Mango is a compact garden hybrid bred from L. longipetala and tolerates a bit more summer moisture than most evergreen lewisias while still needing sharp drainage.

directions: Little Mango is a compact, free-flowering hybrid derived from Lewisia longipetala, part of the same breeding line as Little Plum but selected for its distinctive apricot-orange to mango-toned flowers rather than pink or magenta shades. It forms small, glossy evergreen rosettes topped from late spring into summer with clusters of warm-toned blooms held just above the foliage. Like its longipetala parent, it tolerates somewhat more consistent moisture during the growing season than most evergreen lewisia hybrids, though sharp drainage at the crown is still essential to prevent rot. Grow it in a crevice, trough, or raised scree bed in full sun, watering a bit more generously in spring than other Lewisia species while avoiding standing moisture.

common_name: Slieve Donard Blue Poppy (Vigorous Perennial Himalayan Blue Poppy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade in cool, humid climates; unlike seed-grown blue poppy hybrids, Slieve Donard is a sterile clone propagated only by division and does not die after flowering, forming a long-lived perennial clump.

directions: Raised at the historic Slieve Donard Nursery in Newcastle, County Down, Northern Ireland, this named clone of the Himalayan blue poppy hybrid (M. betonicifolia x M. grandis) is prized because, unlike most seed-grown blue poppies, it is vigorous and reliably perennial rather than monocarpic - it does not exhaust itself and die after flowering. Sterile and propagated only by division, it produces the same enormous, saturated sky-blue to cerulean-blue saucer-shaped flowers with a central boss of golden stamens on tall leafy stems in late spring and early summer. As with the species, success depends on cool, humid summers, acidic and constantly moist but excellently drained soil, and protection from hot, dry, or alkaline conditions. Established clumps can be lifted and divided every three to four years in spring, just as new growth emerges, to maintain vigor and propagate new plants.

common_name: Blue Vase Juniper (Upright Vase-Shaped Blue-Foliage Juniper)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Vase forms an upright, vase-shaped outline of silvery blue-green foliage and, like other Chinese juniper cultivars, tolerates heat, drought, and poor alkaline soils far better than wet, poorly drained conditions.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Blue Vase is an upright Chinese juniper cultivar with strongly ascending branches that flare outward with age into a distinctive open vase shape, clothed in dense, silvery-blue scale-like foliage. Its narrower, structured habit makes it a useful vertical accent or informal screen where a more architectural profile than the broad, flat-topped Pfitzer types is wanted, while still offering the same tough, low-maintenance constitution shared by Chinese juniper cultivars. It is exceptionally tolerant of dry, poor, alkaline soils, heat, and cold, but like other junipers is intolerant of soggy, poorly drained sites and benefits from full sun and good air circulation to reduce fungal blight risk in humid climates.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained, deep, fertile to average soil in full sun; Lucombe oak is a vigorous, fast-growing hybrid that tolerates a wide range of soils, including heavier clays, better than most large evergreen oaks.

directions: Lucombe oak is a naturally occurring hybrid between Turkey oak (Quercus cerris) and cork oak (Quercus suber), first raised in 1762 by nurseryman William Lucombe at his nursery in Exeter, England, and propagated ever since as the clone Lucombeana. It is a majestic, fast-growing, broadly spreading large tree that is semi-evergreen to evergreen in mild winters, holding much of its glossy, coarsely toothed dark-green foliage through the cold season before dropping it as new growth emerges in spring - a trait inherited from its cork oak parent. The bark develops a thick, corky texture with age, also echoing the cork oak side of its parentage, while its vigor and hardiness come chiefly from the Turkey oak parent. Long a favored specimen tree for large parks, estates, and historic gardens in the British Isles, it requires substantial space to accommodate its eventual massive spreading crown and is more tolerant of heavy clay and moderate drought than most large-leaved evergreen oaks.

common_name: Rosea Superba Bower Vine (Large Deep-Pink-Flowered Bower Vine)

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring on a trellis, pergola, fence, or arbor in full sun to partial shade; Rosea Superba grows rapidly in zone 9 and begins blooming in spring, producing larger, deeper-colored flowers than the standard 'Rosea' form. It is more cold-tolerant than many tropical vines, surviving brief dips to 28F.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil; Rosea Superba is a selection of Bower Vine bred for larger, more substantially textured flowers in a deeper rose-pink than the standard 'Rosea' cultivar, with the same rich rose-red throat that gives the flowers their striking two-tone effect. It shares the vigorous, twining, evergreen habit of the species, with fine-textured pinnately compound foliage that forms an airy, dark-green canopy over trellises, pergolas, and arbors. Flowering is heaviest in spring with intermittent bloom through the warm months, and the lightly fragrant flowers are most abundant in full sun, though the vine tolerates and even benefits from afternoon shade in the most intense summer heat. Like other Pandorea jasminoides cultivars it is relatively free of pests and diseases and is a reliable, low-maintenance choice for zone 9-11 gardens.
